notes: Modern plastome analyses place L. guilinensis in the close Clade-IV neighborhood of L. indica, including sister/near-sister resolutions. Species morphology is dimorphic, so the nearest molecular neighborhood fails the frozen negative-architecture gate before ecological eligibility matters.

A broad plastome/coalescent analysis places L. guilinensis plus L. excelsa sister to L. indica in one supported result. L. excelsa has dimorphic fertile stamens, so close phylogenetic position cannot satisfy the absence gate.
L. glabra occurs in the same broad plastome Clade IV as L. indica but has dimorphic stamens. It is retained as an explicit close-relative rejection.

Clade III is sister to the L. indica-containing Clade IV in the registered plastome study. L. subcostata directly shows long and short fertile-stamen sets, so widening one major clade does not yield a negative control.

Floral treatments describe 40-60 monomorphic stamens. Apis cerana honey analyses identify L. parviflora as a major nectar source and later field inventories report frequent Apis cerana/mellifera nectar-and-pollen foraging, demonstrating bee resource use but not a source-secure species-level effective-pollination experiment. The species is not sampled in the frozen modern Lagerstroemia plastome phylogenies, so its relative distance to L. indica versus other monomorphic candidates is also unresolved.

Kim et al. identify L. speciosa as one of the genus's monomorphic-stamen/monomorphic-pollen species, and modern floras describe all stamens as about equal length. Species-level field studies identify large bees including Xylocopa and Bombus/Centris as effective pollinators and document open-pollinated fruit set. However, the strong biological receipt cannot override the unresolved placement/eligibility of monomorphic L. parviflora.

Kim et al. identify L. macrocarpa as the other monomorphic-stamen/monomorphic-pollen species in their 39-species survey; modern flora records numerous stamens all about the same length. A 2022 plastome analysis places it with L. speciosa and L. venusta in a major clade separate from L. indica. Direct species-level effective-pollination evidence remains unresolved, and the unsampled monomorphic L. parviflora also prevents closest-eligible ranking.
